analysis.one_liner: Caps rent-to-own store fees and interest at state installment-sale levels and extends federal credit protections to those customers.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by the House Banking Committee chairman and 14 cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote and died in a House subcommittee at the end of the 103rd Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Rent-to-own stores let people take home furniture, appliances, and electronics with weekly payments and no credit check, and customers who make every payment end up owning the item. The bill would have treated those contracts like installment sales: stores could not charge more interest or fees than state law allows on a regular installment sale, tags and contracts would have to show the cash price, the total cost to own, and an annual percentage rate, and federal laws against abusive debt collection and credit discrimination would apply. It was never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Rent-to-own customers, whom the bill's findings describe as concentrated in low-income and minority neighborhoods. They would see the true total cost of ownership before signing, pay fees capped at installment-sale levels, get the warranties that apply to credit sales, and gain the right to sue violators for damages and attorney fees.

how_it_helps.text: Caps interest, finance charges, and fees at what state law allows for a regular installment sale of the same item, and caps termination fees at 5% of the cash price.
Requires price tags and written contracts to show the cash price, the annual percentage rate, the payment amount, and the total number of payments needed to own the item.

Applies the Truth in Lending Act, Equal Credit Opportunity Act, Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, and Fair Credit Reporting Act to rent-to-own transactions, and bars threats, harassment, and criminal-prosecution threats during collections.
Makes violations enforceable by the Federal Trade Commission and gives customers the right to sue for actual damages plus $250 to $2,500 per violation plus attorney fees.

analysis.who_pays: Rent-to-own dealers, whose business model has historically relied on charges far above installment-sale rates; they would face lower fees, disclosure costs, and lawsuit exposure. Some customers who rely on no-credit-check weekly rentals could face fewer stores or tighter terms if dealers exit.

drawbacks.text: Applying installment-sale interest caps to rent-to-own leases could push some stores out of business or raise upfront costs, reducing access for customers who cannot qualify for any credit and rely on the flexibility of returning an item at any time.

Rent-to-own operators have long argued their products are leases rather than credit sales, so treating them like installment loans imposes disclosure and liability costs on a business model built on terminable weekly rentals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core benefit is large for the people who use these stores: a customer who pays week after week for a television or refrigerator would finally see the true total cost and an annual rate, and could not be charged more than a regular installment buyer. The main cost falls on the dealers, with a real risk that some low-income customers would have fewer rental options if marginal stores closed. On balance the protections outweigh that cost, though the state-by-state caps make the benefit uneven depending on where a customer lives.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking Committee and then to its consumer credit subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or markup until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry B. Gonzalez introduced the Rent-To-Own Reform Act of 1993 on September 27, 1993, and it was referred to the House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs the same day.
Fourteen members cosponsored the bill, 13 Democrats and 1 Republican.
On October 18, 1993, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Credit and Insurance, and the record shows no further action before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

The bill's own findings state that the rent-to-own industry targets low-income and minority neighborhoods, that most customers intend to own the goods, and that dealers often fail to disclose key terms and charge excessive fees and interest rates.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rent-to-own dealers are better off: with no hearing and no vote, they continued operating without federal fee caps, price-tag disclosures, annual-rate disclosures, or liability for abusive collection practices.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill, letting it die in subcommittee at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic (13 of 14 cosponsors), but no committee or floor vote was ever recorded, so opposition never took a measurable form.

industries.note: The bill caps their charges at state installment-sale levels and requires full price and rate disclosure, directly cutting the gap between what customers pay and the cash price of the goods. Dealers' revenue depends on customers paying multiples of an item's cash price, so their interest runs against the customers the bill protects.

The bill applies the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to rent-to-own payments and bans threats, harassment, and criminal-prosecution threats, removing practices some collectors used on this customer base.
The bill would hand the FTC new enforcement authority over rent-to-own transactions, treating violations as unfair or deceptive practices, adding workload but also enforcement tools.
